found.lens: Gravitational-wave and precision-detector experiment (LIGO/Virgo, LISA, PTAs, CMB receivers, microwave axion haloscopes): the literature where a single dimensionless symbol — h, A, T_sys, g_aγγ, Q — silently carries a detector-response, averaging, frame, or noise-bookkeeping convention that no dimensional check can see.
found.overall: The tool's core engine, refuse classes, and 21-fork registry already cover the theory-side notation I meet (8πG, ħ=c=1, geometrized, little-h, signature). What it does not cover is the class that dominates my field: quantities that are dimensionless or dimensionally identical across variants but differ by a *calibration* factor that comes from how the detector was averaged, which frame the symbol lives in, or which piece of the noise budget is counted. Round 3 already claims the spectral family (Fourier/PSD/analytic signal), which is the closest neighbour — everything below is on top of a fixed PSD convention and is orthogonal to it. Two structural asks recur: (a) a "sky/orientation-averaging state" that behaves like the E&M riders (a factor that must be applied to h or √S_n and is invisible once applied), and (b) a per-symbol *frame* tag (source vs detector, i.e. (1+z)), which is the single most common silent factor in compact-binary papers and has no dimensional signature at all. The GW community itself has a review paper (Moore, Cole & Berry 2015, CQG 32 015014) written for no reason other than that these conventions are routinely confused, which is about as strong an evidence base as a convention gap gets. I have deliberately not listed things that reduce to the excluded one-sided/two-sided PSD fork (e.g. the 4 in ρ² = 4∫|h̃|²/S_n df, or ℒ(f) = ½S_φ(f) in oscillator phase noise), nor the dB/dex family (squeezing in dB, dBc/Hz, magnitudes), which is correctly refused.

gaps.name: Sky-, polarization- and inclination-averaging state of a quoted strain or noise curve
gaps.what_breaks: A quoted h, a plotted √S_n, or a quoted detector range is one of several angle-averaging states — optimally oriented/overhead, sky-and-polarization averaged, or sky-inclination-orientation averaged — with no dimensional difference between them. The tool will happily equate an 'optimal' amplitude from a source paper with an 'averaged' sensitivity curve from a detector paper and report agreement when the two differ by a factor of 2–2.5. Dimensional analysis cannot see it because the averaging factor is a pure number multiplying a dimensionless strain (or a rider on √S_n with units unchanged). It is also not a Fourier/PSD issue: it survives after the PSD convention is fixed.
gaps.magnitude: For an L-shaped (90°) interferometer, ⟨F₊²⟩ = ⟨F×²⟩ = 1/5 and ⟨F₊²+F×²⟩ = 2/5 over sky and polarization; including inclination for an inspiral, ⟨(F₊(1+cos²ι)/2)² + (F× cos ι)²⟩ = 4/25, so the rms averaged amplitude is 2/5 of the optimal one (factor 2.5 in amplitude, 6.25 in SNR). The volume-preserving 'range' vs 'horizon distance' factor is 2.264 (Finn & Chernoff). 'Sky-averaged' LISA curves carry an extra √5 inflation of √S_n relative to the sky-localized instrument curve, plus a 3/20 (not 1/5) response for 60° arms.
gaps.example: Detector paper: 'the sky-averaged sensitivity is √S_n(100 Hz) = 4×10⁻²⁴ Hz^{-1/2}' — this already contains the ×√5 penalty. Source paper: 'an optimally oriented, overhead binary at 400 Mpc gives h = 1×10⁻²²' — this contains no penalty. LIGO papers quote 'BNS range 160 Mpc' while the same detector's horizon distance is 160×2.264 = 362 Mpc; a tool that treats 'range' and 'maximum detectable distance' as the same symbol is off by 2.26 in distance and 11.6 in rate.
gaps.fingerprint: Look for the literal tokens 'sky-averaged', 'angle-averaged', 'orientation-averaged', 'optimally oriented', 'face-on', 'overhead', 'horizon distance', 'range', 'sensemon', 'effective distance D_eff'; for the presence of F₊/F× or a detector response function in the equation being read; for the numbers 1/5, 2/5, 4/25, 3/20, √5, 2.26, 0.442 appearing as bare constants; and for LISA papers, whether the quoted curve is 'instrument', 'sky-averaged', or 'sensitivity including the averaged response'. Absence of any such token in a source-amplitude formula is itself the fingerprint for 'optimal'.

gaps.name: Interferometer/timing strain response normalization: h = ΔL/L differential vs δL/L per arm, and the detector-tensor ½
gaps.what_breaks: 'Strain' is defined either as the differential arm-length change of the full Michelson (h = (δL_x − δL_y)/L) or as the fractional length change of one arm (δL_x/L). These differ by exactly 2 and are both written 'h = ΔL/L' in prose. The same fork appears as the detector tensor written D^{ab} = ½(x̂^a x̂^b − ŷ^a ŷ^b) vs (x̂^a x̂^b − ŷ^a ŷ^b), and in Doppler/pulsar-timing as one-way vs round-trip fractional frequency shift. Both variants are dimensionless, so the solve and the residual-rank check pass either way; the tool would silently convert a calibrated displacement noise into a strain noise off by 2.
gaps.magnitude: Exactly a factor of 2 in strain (4 in S_h, 4 in inferred GW energy density, 2 in inferred source distance).
gaps.example: Variant A (standard LIGO): for h₊ incident along z, δL_x = +½h₊L and δL_y = −½h₊L, so h ≡ (δL_x − δL_y)/L = h₊, with D^{ab} = ½(x̂x̂ − ŷŷ)^{ab} and h = D^{ab}h_{ab}. Variant B (per-arm/optics papers): h ≡ δL_x/L = ½h₊, i.e. 'a 10⁻²¹ wave moves a 4 km arm by 4×10⁻¹⁸ m' vs Variant A's 'moves the differential arm by 4×10⁻¹⁸ m' — the same sentence, half the physical displacement.
gaps.fingerprint: Presence or absence of the ½ in the detector tensor; whether the response equation subtracts two arms; whether the text says 'differential arm motion (DARM)' or 'arm length change'; in the numbers, whether δL = hL or δL = hL/2 is used to convert a displacement-noise ASD (m/√Hz) into a strain ASD; in PTA/Doppler, 'one-way' vs 'two-way/round-trip' and whether the redshift z(t) formula carries a ½.

gaps.name: The sensitivity-curve quantity family: h_c vs h_n = √(f S_h) vs √S_h vs S_h vs Ω_gw — and the h_c ↔ h̃ constant
gaps.what_breaks: Five different quantities are plotted on the same log–log axes and all called 'the strain'. Two of them (h_c and h_n = √(f S_h)) are dimensionless and cannot be told apart dimensionally; the tool would treat a source's h_c curve and a detector's √S_n curve as comparable when they differ by a frequency-dependent √f, and would compare an Ω_gw(f) constraint with an h_c constraint with no conversion. Worse, the definition of h_c itself forks: h_c² = 4f²|h̃(f)|² (Moore–Cole–Berry) vs h_c² = 2f²|h̃(f)|² appears in the literature, a bare factor 2 in power.
gaps.magnitude: √f between h_c and √S_h (i.e. ~10× at f = 100 Hz if the units are Hz^{-1/2} — a dimension shift the tool can catch — but 1× dimensionally between h_c and h_n, which it cannot); factor 2 in h_c² (√2 ≈ 1.41 in amplitude) between the two h_c definitions; the h_c ↔ Ω map carries the constant 2π²/3H₀² so an error in H₀ convention or in h_c definition propagates as a factor 2 into Ω_gw.
gaps.example: Variant A: h_c(f) ≡ √(f S_h(f)), Ω_gw(f) = (2π²/3H₀²) f² h_c²(f), and for a burst h_c² = 4f²|h̃(f)|². Variant B (common in PTA/space-detector plots): 'characteristic strain' h_c² = 2f²|h̃(f)|², or the noise curve plotted as h_n(f) = √(f S_n(f)) and labelled 'characteristic strain of the noise' — putting a source h_c and a detector h_n on the same axes is intentional and correct, but reading either as √S_n is a Hz^{1/2} error and reading one h_c convention as the other is a factor √2.
gaps.fingerprint: Axis label and units: 'Hz^{-1/2}' ⇒ amplitude spectral density; dimensionless ⇒ h_c or h_n; presence of the defining relation h_c = √(fS) vs h_c = 2f|h̃| in the text; the constants 4f², 2f², 2π²/3 appearing near the symbol; the phrase 'characteristic strain'. A converter should refuse silently equating h_c and √S_n and instead emit the explicit √f (and the declared h_c definition).

gaps.name: PTA background amplitude: A in characteristic strain vs A in timing-residual power spectrum, and γ vs α
gaps.what_breaks: Post-2023 nanohertz papers quote 'A' with two incompatible meanings and two incompatible spectral indices. A_h_c is the dimensionless characteristic-strain amplitude at f = 1 yr⁻¹; A_red is the amplitude of the timing-residual power spectral density, which has units of s³ (or yr³) and is related by a bare 12π². The exponent is quoted either as α (strain index) or γ (PSD index) with γ = 3 − 2α, so the canonical SMBHB value is α = −2/3 *or* γ = 13/3 for the same physics. A tool that restores dimensions will notice the s³ vs dimensionless difference only if the paper states units, which many do not; and it has no way at all to know whether an exponent labelled with a bare Greek letter is α or γ.
gaps.magnitude: 12π² ≈ 118.4 in power spectral density (≈10.9 in amplitude), plus f_yr^{-3} = (3.156×10⁷ s)^{-3} if the reference is not stated; sign and value flip between α = −2/3 and γ = +13/3.
gaps.example: Variant A: h_c(f) = A (f/f_yr)^α with A = 2.4×10⁻¹⁵, α = −2/3. Variant B: the cross-spectral density of residuals S_{ab}(f) = Γ_{ab} h_c²(f)/(12π² f³) = (A_red²/12π²) f_yr^{-3} (f/f_yr)^{-γ} with γ = 13/3; a paper reporting 'log₁₀A = −14.6' is unusable unless it is known which of the two A's, and PTA collaborations report both in different tables of the same paper.
gaps.fingerprint: Units on A (dimensionless vs s³ or yr³ vs yr^{3/2}); the exponent letter and whether the reported posterior clusters near −2/3 or near 13/3 (sign alone disambiguates); presence of the constant 12π², of f_yr or 'yr⁻¹' as a reference frequency, or of 'red noise'/'timing residual' near the symbol; 'log₁₀A_GWB' with a value near −15 (strain) vs near −14 with s³ units.

gaps.name: Overlap reduction function normalization (Hellings–Downs Γ(0) = ½ vs 1; interferometer γ(f) with or without the 1/5)
gaps.what_breaks: The angular correlation function that multiplies the background power is normalized differently across papers, and it is dimensionless, so the tool cannot detect a rescaling that propagates directly into the inferred background amplitude. Two independent forks: (i) in PTA, the Hellings–Downs function is normalized so that Γ(ζ→0) = 1/2 for distinct pulsars, with Γ_aa = 1 for the autocorrelation (pulsar term), vs a rescaled convention normalized to Γ(0) = 1; (ii) for ground-based cross-correlation, the overlap reduction function γ(f) is defined either with the 1/5 sky-average factor absorbed so that γ(0) = 1 for coincident co-aligned detectors, or without it so that γ(0) = 2/5.
gaps.magnitude: Factor 2 in the correlation, hence √2 ≈ 1.41 (41%) in the inferred amplitude A; factor 5/2 in the interferometer case, hence 1.58 in amplitude. Both are inside or comparable to current PTA and LVK error bars, so the mis-scaling is not obviously absurd — the worst kind.
gaps.example: Variant A (NANOGrav/EPTA): Γ_ab(ζ) = ½ − (1/4)x + (3/2)x ln x with x = (1−cos ζ)/2, giving Γ → 1/2 as ζ → 0, plus δ_ab/2 for the pulsar term (so Γ_aa = 1). Variant B: the same shape multiplied by 2 so that the curve starts at 1 and reaches −1/2 at 180°, with the factor absorbed into the reported A². For LVK: Ω_gw estimator with γ(f) normalized to γ(0)=1 vs γ(0)=2/5 (Allen–Romano vs the un-normalized detector-response form).
gaps.fingerprint: The stated value of the ORF at zero separation (0.5 vs 1.0) and at 180° (−0.25 vs −0.5); whether a δ_ab pulsar term is written and with what coefficient (1/2 vs 1); for interferometers, whether γ(0) is quoted as 1 or 0.4, and whether a separate 1/5 appears elsewhere in the estimator.

gaps.name: Source frame vs detector frame: redshifted masses, frequencies and times
gaps.what_breaks: In compact-binary and PTA literature the same symbols M, M_chirp, f, t carry an implicit frame: detector-frame (redshifted) quantities are (1+z) times the source-frame ones for masses and 1/(1+z) times for frequencies. There is no dimensional, unit-system, or numeric-value signature — both are kilograms or solar masses, both are hertz. The tool would translate a waveform equation written in detector-frame variables into 'physical' source parameters and be wrong by a factor that varies event to event. This is not the comoving/little-h axis already covered: it is a per-symbol frame qualifier on mass and frequency, not a cosmological distance scaling.
gaps.magnitude: (1+z): ~1.1 for nearby LIGO events, ~2 for the loudest, up to ~10–20 for LISA massive-black-hole binaries and for PTA sources and primordial-background frequency mapping. Chirp mass errors of 10–100%; a source-frame mass function inferred from detector-frame masses is shifted by exactly this factor.
gaps.example: Variant A (detector frame, what appears in the waveform): h(f) ∝ M_c^{5/6}/D_L · f^{-7/6} with M_c ≡ (1+z)M_c^{src} and D_L the luminosity distance — the (1+z) is hidden because the combination M_c^{det}/D_L is what the data constrain. Variant B (source frame): the same formula with M_c^{src} and an explicit (1+z)^{5/6} factor, or with D_L replaced by the comoving distance and an explicit redshift factor. GW150914 is quoted as '65 M_⊙ total detector-frame / 62 M_⊙ source-frame' — a tool that restores constants in the first equation and reports 'total mass' has no way to say which.
gaps.fingerprint: The literal qualifiers 'detector frame', 'redshifted', 'source frame', 'intrinsic'; whether D_L or comoving distance appears (D_L pairs with detector-frame masses in the standard amplitude); whether (1+z) appears explicitly anywhere in the amplitude or phase; symbol decorations M^{det}/M_z/M^z vs M^{src}; a reported mass posterior with both a 'detector-frame' and 'source-frame' row.

gaps.name: Axion–photon coupling normalization: g_γ vs C_aγγ, f_a vs f_PQ/N, and the FF̃ prefactor
gaps.what_breaks: Haloscope and astrophysics papers report 'the axion-photon coupling' in at least three normalizations that all have dimensions of inverse energy (or are dimensionless in the g_γ case), so dimensional restoration cannot distinguish them; converting a bound quoted in one to a limit plotted in another is a bare factor 2 (or 4, or the domain-wall number N). The tool would restore ħ, c into either form and certify both.
gaps.magnitude: Factor 2 between g_γ and C_aγγ = E/N − 1.92 (g_γ = C_aγγ/2); factor N (domain-wall number: N = 1 for KSVZ, N = 3 or 6 for DFSZ depending on generation counting) between f_a and f_PQ; factor 4 when the Lagrangian is written without the 1/4 on FF̃. Combined worst case ~an order of magnitude on the plotted coupling axis.
gaps.example: Variant A: L = −(1/4) g_aγγ a F_{μν}F̃^{μν} = g_aγγ a E·B with g_aγγ = (α/2π f_a)(E/N − 1.92). Variant B: L = −g_γ (α/π)(1/f_a) a E·B with g_γ = 0.36 (DFSZ) or −0.97 (KSVZ), i.e. g_aγγ = α g_γ/(π (f_PQ/N)). Reading 'g = 0.36' from B as a value of C_aγγ (whose DFSZ value is 0.75) is a factor 2; reading f_a in B as f_PQ is a further factor N.
gaps.fingerprint: Whether the reported coupling is dimensionless (⇒ g_γ) or in GeV⁻¹ (⇒ g_aγγ); the constants 1.92, 1.92(4), 0.36, 0.97, 0.75, −1.95 appearing near the definition; the presence of 'E/N', 'anomaly', 'domain wall number N', 'f_PQ' vs 'f_a'; the prefactor on FF̃ (1/4 present or absent) and whether the Lagrangian is written in E·B form. The ε-convention needed to map FF̃ → −4E·B is already on the covered sign axis, but the 1/4 and the g_γ↔C factor are not.

gaps.name: Noise-temperature bookkeeping: whether the ½-photon vacuum term is inside T_sys, and Rayleigh–Jeans-defined vs Callen–Welton temperature
gaps.what_breaks: 'System noise temperature' is a kelvin either way, so dimensional analysis is blind, but papers differ on (i) whether the hν/2 zero-point term is counted inside T_sys or moved to the signal side, (ii) whether T_sys is defined by the Rayleigh–Jeans relation P = k_B T B (valid only for hν ≪ k_B T) or by the full Callen–Welton occupation, and (iii) whether the amplifier noise is reported as an added photon number N_A (dimensionless) or a temperature. In the quantum-limited regime these are not small corrections: the RJ definition and the photon-occupation definition disagree by order unity precisely where haloscopes operate.
gaps.magnitude: At 5 GHz, hν/k_B = 0.240 K, so the ½-photon vacuum term is 0.120 K against dilution-fridge cavity temperatures of ~0.1 K — a factor up to ~2 in T_sys and, since haloscope scan rate ∝ T_sys⁻², up to a factor 4 in quoted scan rate or exclusion reach. T_SQL = hν/k_B (½ vacuum + ½ added) vs 'quantum-limited amplifier noise = hν/2k_B' is the same factor-2 fork.
gaps.example: Variant A (full): k_B T_sys = hν[ 1/(e^{hν/k_BT} − 1) + 1/2 + N_A ]. Variant B (RJ/amplifier-only): T_sys = T_cav + T_amp with T_cav the physical temperature and no ½. At ν = 5 GHz, T = 100 mK: variant A gives k_B T_sys/hν = 0.09 + 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.09 → T_sys = 0.26 K; variant B gives 0.1 + 0.12 = 0.22 K, and a naive RJ reading of the thermal term (T_cav = 0.1 K instead of the true occupation 0.09×0.240 = 0.022 K) compounds the error.
gaps.fingerprint: Presence of the Bose factor 1/(e^{hν/k_BT}−1) vs a bare T; an explicit '+1/2' or 'zero-point'/'vacuum'/'Callen–Welton' in the noise expression; whether the amplifier is characterized by N_A (photons, dimensionless) or T_amp (K); whether T_SQL is quoted as hν/k_B or hν/2k_B; the Dicke radiometer equation written with T_sys vs with photon occupation n̄.

gaps.name: Brightness temperature kind: K_RJ vs thermodynamic K_CMB (and antenna temperature)
gaps.what_breaks: CMB and mm-wave papers report amplitudes 'in μK' under two different definitions — Rayleigh–Jeans (antenna) temperature, defined by I_ν = 2k_B T_RJ ν²/c², and thermodynamic CMB temperature, defined by the derivative of the Planck function at T_CMB = 2.7255 K. Both are kelvin. A tool converting a map noise level, a foreground amplitude, or a tensor-to-scalar-ratio-related band power between frequency bands will be wrong by a frequency-dependent factor, and will silently combine a 95 GHz number with a 150 GHz number that were quoted in different kinds.
gaps.magnitude: dT_RJ/dT_CMB = x²e^x/(e^x−1)² with x = hν/k_B T_CMB: 0.796 at 95 GHz, 0.576 at 150 GHz, 0.334 at 220 GHz. So 1 μK_CMB = 0.58 μK_RJ at 150 GHz — a 1.74× error, and the error is different in every band, which is exactly what corrupts a spectral-index fit for dust or synchrotron.
gaps.example: Variant A: 'the polarized dust amplitude is 4.6 μK_CMB² at 353 GHz'. Variant B: 'A_d = 4.6 μK_RJ² at 353 GHz'. At 353 GHz x = 6.22 and the conversion is 0.0714, so the two statements differ by a factor ~200 in power. A converter that treats both as 'kelvin squared' would pass a dimensional check and produce nonsense.
gaps.fingerprint: Subscripts/suffixes 'K_CMB', 'K_RJ', 'μK-arcmin (CMB)', 'antenna temperature', 'T_A'; the presence of the conversion factor x²e^x/(e^x−1)² or the phrase 'thermodynamic units'; the constant 2.7255 K; a foreground spectral index quoted as β_d ≈ 1.5 (RJ, modified blackbody in intensity) which only makes sense in intensity/RJ units.

gaps.name: Resonator rate conventions: loaded vs unloaded Q with coupling β, and κ/g as FWHM vs half-width vs splitting
gaps.what_breaks: In cavity haloscope, optomechanics and circuit-QED papers, 'Q' and the linewidth/coupling rates are quoted in mutually inconsistent normalizations that are all dimensionally identical (Q dimensionless; κ, g in rad/s or Hz). The Sikivie haloscope power formula P ∝ Q is written with Q_0 (unloaded), Q_L (loaded), or min(Q, Q_a), with a separate β/(1+β) coupling factor that some papers absorb and some do not; κ is defined as the FWHM energy decay rate in some papers and as the amplitude/half-width rate in others; and 'g' is either the vacuum coupling rate or the observed normal-mode splitting, which is 2g.
gaps.magnitude: Q_0 = (1+β)Q_L, so a factor 2 at critical coupling (β = 1) and more when over-coupled (β = 2 gives 3); β/(1+β) = 1/2 at critical coupling, another factor 2 in signal power. κ FWHM vs half-width: factor 2. g vs 2g splitting: factor 2. Compounded, quoted haloscope signal powers or cooperativities C = 4g²/κγ (vs g²/κγ) differ by up to 4.
gaps.example: Variant A: P_sig = g_aγγ² (ρ_a/m_a) B₀² V C_{nml} Q_L · β/(1+β), with Q_L the loaded quality factor measured from the FWHM of the transmission dip. Variant B: the same expression written with Q_0 and no explicit β factor, 'assuming critical coupling'. At β = 1 these differ by exactly 2 in Q and 2 in the coupling factor. Similarly C = 4g²/(κγ) (Aspelmeyer–Kippenberg) vs C = g²/(κγ).
gaps.fingerprint: Subscripts on Q (Q_0, Q_L, Q_U, Q_a) and whether β, 'coupling coefficient', 'critically coupled', 'reflection coefficient' appear; whether the linewidth is called FWHM, HWHM, 'energy decay rate', or 'amplitude decay rate'; whether a measured splitting is reported as 2g/2π or g/2π; the presence of the factor 4 in the cooperativity definition. Note this is not the ν-vs-ω/radian-collapse fork already covered — it persists after the angular-frequency convention is fixed.

verdict.lens: Gravitational-wave and precision-detector experiment (LIGO/Virgo, LISA, PTAs, CMB receivers, microwave axion haloscopes) — dimensionless or dimensionally-identical symbols carrying silent detector-response, averaging, frame, or noise-bookkeeping calibration factors.

verdicts.gap: Sky-, polarization- and inclination-averaging state of a quoted strain or noise curve
verdicts.notes: Recomputed and correct. Sky+polarization average for a 90 deg L-shaped IFO: <F+^2>=<Fx^2>=1/5, sum 2/5. Adding inclination for an inspiral: <((1+cos^2 i)/2)^2> = 7/15 and <cos^2 i> = 1/3 over uniform cos i, so (1/5)(7/15+5/15) = (1/5)(4/5) = 4/25; rms/optimal amplitude = 2/5, i.e. 2.5 in amplitude and 6.25 in SNR. Finn-Chernoff range-to-horizon 2.264 and 2.264^3 = 11.6 in rate both check. Not in coverage (no averaging-state axis anywhere) and not in the round-3 exclusions; correctly argued to survive after the one-sided/two-sided and Fourier conventions are fixed, so it is not the spectral family. One correction to the LISA sentence: it conflates two factors. The sqrt(5) is the sky-and-polarization average alone; the 60 deg arm geometry supplies a further 3/4, giving the standard low-frequency sky-averaged response R = 3/20 and an inflation of sqrt(20/3) = 2.58 on sqrt(S_n), not sqrt(5). Fix that in the entry text; registry_entry / v1 stands.

verdicts.gap: Interferometer/timing strain response normalization: h = dL/L differential vs dL/L per arm, and the detector-tensor 1/2
verdicts.notes: Factor 2 verified: for h+ along z, dL_x = +h+L/2 and dL_y = -h+L/2, so DARM/L = h+ while per-arm dL_x/L = h+/2. Not in coverage or exclusions. Prevalence caveat: the 'detector tensor written without the 1/2' variant is the weakest leg — D^ab = (1/2)(xx - yy) is close to universal in the response literature, and writing it without the 1/2 reads more as an error than an established fork. The two load-bearing real instances are (i) converting a calibrated displacement-noise ASD in m/rtHz into a strain ASD (dL = hL vs dL = hL/2) and (ii) one-way pulsar timing vs two-way spacecraft Doppler tracking, where the round-trip z(t) genuinely carries the extra 1/2. Write the entry around those two and demote the detector-tensor line to a fingerprint rather than a claimed variant.

verdicts.gap: The sensitivity-curve quantity family: h_c vs h_n = sqrt(f S_h) vs sqrt(S_h) vs S_h vs Omega_gw — and the h_c <-> h~ constant
verdicts.notes: Three of the four asserted failure modes are not silent. (a) h_c vs sqrt(S_h) differs by Hz^{1/2} — a dimension shift the existing solve already catches, as the claim itself concedes. (b) h_c and h_n = sqrt(f S_n) are not inter-convertible quantities at all; plotting a source h_c against a detector h_n on one axis is correct by construction, so there is no factor to get wrong. (c) The h_c^2 = 4 f^2 |h~|^2 vs 2 f^2 |h~|^2 factor of 2 traces to the one-sided vs two-sided spectral convention, which is round-3 exclusion (2) — it has exactly the same origin as the 4 in rho^2 = 4 integral |h~|^2/S_n that the critic himself correctly excluded, so excluding one and claiming the other is inconsistent. Omega_gw = (2 pi^2 / 3 H0^2) f^2 h_c^2 is verified and correct. Corrected claim: what remains worth adding is a small numeric-converter triangle h_c <-> S_h <-> Omega_gw (plus a kind label distinguishing h_c from h_n), which is one converter edge on the existing equivalence graph, not a v1 convention fork. Downgrade to converter edge, v2.

verdicts.gap: PTA background amplitude: A in characteristic strain vs A in timing-residual power spectrum, and gamma vs alpha
verdicts.notes: The exponent half is right: S ∝ h_c^2/f^3 with h_c ∝ f^alpha gives S ∝ f^(2 alpha - 3), so gamma = 3 - 2 alpha and alpha = -2/3 <-> gamma = 13/3. Verified. The amplitude half is misdescribed. In the dominant NANOGrav/enterprise parameterization S(f) = (A^2/12 pi^2)(f/f_yr)^(-gamma) yr^3, the yr^3 is written explicitly and A is dimensionless — it is the characteristic-strain amplitude at f_yr — and pulsar-intrinsic A_red is the same kind of object, so the claimed 'dimensionless vs s^3' contrast is not the standard fork. The real (and rarer) fork is whether the yr^3 is absorbed into the amplitude, which makes A carry yr^(3/2); its size is f_yr^(3/2), not 12 pi^2. 12 pi^2 is a fixed definitional constant appearing identically in both variants, so 'a 12 pi^2 = 118 error in PSD, 10.9 in amplitude' is not a conversion the tool would actually make. Corrected claim: the entry should be (A, alpha) <-> (A, gamma) exponent-label translation plus a reference-frequency / yr^3-absorbed tag, and should also flag that A is gamma-dependent (a fixed-gamma = 13/3 posterior and a varied-gamma posterior report different A for the same data). Converter entry is the right slot; v1 is defensible only for the exponent half.

verdicts.gap: Overlap reduction function normalization (Hellings-Downs Gamma(0) = 1/2 vs 1; interferometer gamma(f) with or without the 1/5)
verdicts.notes: The PTA normalization fork is real: Gamma_ab = (1/2)delta_ab + 1/2 - x/4 + (3/2) x ln x with x = (1-cos z)/2 gives Gamma -> 1/2 as z -> 0 for distinct pulsars and Gamma_aa = 1 with the pulsar term, and a doubled convention exists. But a stated number is wrong and would make the fingerprint misfire. At z = 180 deg, x = 1 and x ln x = 0, so Gamma(pi) = 1/2 - 1/4 = +1/4, POSITIVE, not -1/4; in the doubled normalization it is +1/2, not -1/2. The curve's minimum is about -0.15 near z = 82 deg and it rises back through zero to +1/4. Any detector keyed on 'reaches -0.25 vs -0.5 at 180 deg' will never fire. Second issue: the interferometer half (gamma(0) = 1 vs 2/5) is the identical 1/5 sky-and-polarization average already claimed in gap 1 — an internal duplicate. Corrected claim: keep only the PTA Gamma(0) = 1/2 vs 1 fork (factor 2 in correlation, sqrt(2) = 1.41 in inferred A), fix the 180 deg value to +1/4 / +1/2, and fold the interferometer 5/2 into gap 1's averaging state. v2 is right for what survives.

verdicts.gap: Source frame vs detector frame: redshifted masses, frequencies and times
verdicts.notes: Real, common, and genuinely invisible: M_det = (1+z) M_src, f_det = f_src/(1+z), both sides in kg or M_sun and Hz, with no dimensional, unit-system, or numeric signature. Correctly distinguished from the covered little-h / comoving axis — those rescale distances and have a per-symbol exponent map; this is a per-symbol frame qualifier on mass, frequency and time and is orthogonal to them. Not in the round-3 exclusions. schema_feature / v1 is the right slot: mechanically it is the same shape as the existing little-h per-symbol exponent map, a tag that propagates through the solve rather than a numeric fork. One factual fix to the example: 65 M_sun is GW150914's SOURCE-frame total mass (36 + 29); at z = 0.09 the detector-frame total is about 70.6 M_sun. The quoted '65 detector / 62 source' pairing implies z = 0.05 and is not the published pair — swap it for 65 source / ~70.6 detector.

verdicts.gap: Axion-photon coupling normalization: g_gamma vs C_agammagamma, f_a vs f_PQ/N, and the FFdual prefactor
verdicts.notes: Two of the three sub-forks are real and uncovered. Verified: g_agg = (alpha/2 pi f_a) C_agg with C_agg = E/N - 1.92; DFSZ E/N = 8/3 gives C = 0.746 and g_gamma = C/2 = 0.373, matching the quoted 0.36 when -1.95 is used instead of -1.92; KSVZ E/N = 0 gives C = -1.92 and g_gamma = -0.96. So the factor-2 g_gamma <-> C_agg fork is exact, and f_a = f_PQ/N with N = 1 (KSVZ) or 3/6 (DFSZ, generation counting) is a genuine second factor. Neither is in the 21-fork registry, which has the analogous M_Pl-vs-reduced and vev-246-vs-174 entries but nothing axion. Trim one sub-piece: the '1/4 on a F Fdual' prefactor is an interaction-term normalization, i.e. round-3 exclusion (3) (the lambda phi^4/4! family) — drop it from this entry and let the excluded item carry it. The critic already correctly notes the epsilon convention mapping F Fdual -> -4 E.B is on the covered sign axis. Combined worst case is about x12 (2 x 6), which supports 'order of magnitude' only with the N = 6 DFSZ counting; say so rather than leaving it open.

verdicts.gap: Noise-temperature bookkeeping: whether the 1/2-photon vacuum term is inside T_sys, and Rayleigh-Jeans-defined vs Callen-Welton temperature
verdicts.notes: Arithmetic verified. At 5 GHz, h nu / k_B = 0.2399 K, so the half-photon term is 0.120 K, against 0.1 K physical cavity temperature — the vacuum term genuinely dominates there. Bose occupation at 100 mK: x = 2.399, n = 1/(e^x - 1) = 0.100 (the claim says 0.09; rounding, not an error). Variant A: k_B T_sys / h nu = 0.100 + 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.10 -> T_sys = 0.264 K; variant B: 0.1 + 0.12 = 0.22 K; and the RJ misreading of the thermal term (0.1 K instead of n h nu / k_B = 0.024 K) compounds it as claimed. Scan rate scaling as T_sys^-2 gives up to x4 in quoted reach. Not in coverage — the registry's k_B = 1 and spectroscopic-equivalence entries are about unit identification, not about which terms are counted inside a defined temperature — and not in exclusions. registry_entry / v2 is sensible.

verdicts.gap: Brightness temperature kind: K_RJ vs thermodynamic K_CMB (and antenna temperature)
verdicts.notes: The physics is right but two numbers are off and the gap is mostly already claimed. Recomputed dT_RJ/dT_CMB = x^2 e^x/(e^x - 1)^2 with x = h nu / k_B (2.7255 K): 0.797 at 95 GHz (claim 0.796, fine), 0.577 at 150 GHz (claim 0.576, fine), but 0.325 at 220 GHz — 0.334 is the 217 GHz Planck-band value, so the band label is wrong. At 353 GHz, x = 6.216 gives 0.0775, not 0.0714, so the power ratio is about 167, not 'a factor ~200'. More importantly, the detection mechanism is exactly round-3 exclusion (5): quantity-kind tags on a unit, the Gy-vs-Sv and chi_v/chi_mol/chi_g pattern applied to kelvin (K_CMB / K_RJ / T_A). Once that schema feature exists, the tool already refuses to silently add a 95 GHz number to a 150 GHz number of a different kind. Corrected claim: the only genuinely new content beyond the exclusion is the frequency-dependent conversion function itself, so ship it as one converter edge hanging off the already-claimed kelvin kind tag, not as a standalone v2 gap.

verdicts.gap: Resonator rate conventions: loaded vs unloaded Q with coupling beta, and kappa/g as FWHM vs half-width vs splitting
verdicts.notes: The physics is all correct — Q_0 = (1+beta) Q_L (factor 2 at critical coupling, 3 at beta = 2), beta/(1+beta) = 1/2 at critical coupling, kappa as FWHM energy decay vs half-width amplitude rate is a clean factor 2, the observed vacuum Rabi splitting is 2g, and C = 4g^2/(kappa gamma) vs g^2/(kappa gamma) is a real Aspelmeyer-Kippenberg-vs-other split, compounding to 4. It is also correctly argued to be distinct from the covered h/hbar and nu/omega radian-collapse fork. But rider_table is the wrong slot. Riders in this engine are fixed numeric factors (c, 4 pi) that fire when the factor lies outside the span of restored generators; none of these behave that way. Correct slotting: (i) kappa FWHM-vs-HWHM, the 2g splitting, and the 4 in cooperativity are plain dimensionless numeric forks and belong as registry entries, sitting directly beside the existing radian-collapse fork; (ii) Q_0 vs Q_L is not a numeric fork at all — the ratio depends on the measured coupling beta, so it belongs with the quantity-kind tags (exclusion 5) plus a declared per-paper parameter, structurally the same as a CUSTOM generator declaration with its rank check. Split the entry along that line; v2 for the registry half.

verdict.overall: Strong lens with a real structural contribution, but roughly half the entries need trimming or correction before they are written. Five confirmed: the sky/polarization/inclination averaging state (gap 1), the differential-vs-per-arm strain normalization (gap 2), the source-vs-detector-frame per-symbol tag (gap 6, the single most valuable item here and cleanly orthogonal to the covered little-h/comoving axis), the axion g_gamma/C_agg and f_a/f_PQ forks (gap 7), and the Callen-Welton-vs-Rayleigh-Jeans noise-temperature bookkeeping (gap 8). Four overstated: the sensitivity-curve family (gap 3) collapses to one converter edge once the dimension shift and the one-sided/two-sided origin of its factor 2 are removed — the critic excluded that factor in rho^2 but re-imported it in h_c^2; the PTA amplitude entry (gap 4) has the exponent half right and the units half wrong, since A is dimensionless in the standard enterprise parameterization and 12 pi^2 is a shared constant rather than a fork; the ORF entry (gap 5) states the Hellings-Downs 180 deg value with the wrong sign (+1/4, not -1/4, so its proposed fingerprint would never fire) and its interferometer half duplicates gap 1's 1/5; the CMB brightness-temperature entry (gap 9) is a near-duplicate of the already-excluded quantity-kind-tag feature, with 0.334 mislabeled as 220 GHz and the 353 GHz ratio ~167 rather than ~200. One mis-slotted: the resonator Q/kappa/g conventions (gap 10) are real but split across a registry entry and a quantity-kind tag with a declared beta, not a rider table. The two structural asks the critic leads with — an averaging state and a per-symbol frame tag — both survive verification and are the right things to build.
